q: In an atom the negatively charged electrons are moving around a positively charged nucleus.
e: Electrons, which are negatively charged, orbit the positively charged nucleus of an atom.

q: The electrons closer to the nucleus experience less attractive force of the nucleus.
e: The electrons closer to the nucleus experience a greater attractive force from the nucleus.

q: The electrons closer to the nucleus cannot move freely and are called bound electrons.
e: Due to the strong attractive force, inner electrons are tightly bound and cannot move freely.

q: The electrons far away from the nucleus are loosely bound and are called free electrons.
e: Outer electrons experience less attractive force, making them loosely bound and free to move.

q: Free electrons can move from one atom to another.
e: Because they are loosely bound, free electrons can transfer between atoms.

q: The number of free electrons in a substance depends upon the nature of that substance.
e: Different substances have different atomic structures, which determines the number of free electrons they possess.

q: The substance which has plenty of free electrons is called an insulator.
e: A substance with plenty of free electrons is called a conductor, not an insulator.

q: The substance which has very few or no free electrons is called an insulator.
e: Insulators lack free electrons, which prevents the easy flow of electric charge.
Metals contain many free electrons, making them excellent conductors of electricity.

q: Most non-metals conduct electricity well, although carbon is an exception.
e: Most non-metals conduct electricity poorly or not at all, although carbon is an exception.

q: In insulators all the electrons are held tightly in position and unable to move from atom to atom.
e: The electrons in insulators are tightly bound to their atoms, preventing electrical conduction.

q: Although the electrons are not free to move in insulators, they can be transferred from one object to another.
e: While electrons cannot move freely within an insulator, they can be transferred between different objects, such as by rubbing.

q: Some substances which contain a moderate amount of free electrons are called semiconductors.
e: Semiconductors have an intermediate number of free electrons, placing them between conductors and insulators.

q: Semiconductors are both conductors and insulators.
e: Semiconductors are neither conductors nor insulators; they have properties distinct from both.

q: Silicon and germanium are widely used as semiconductors.
e: Silicon and germanium are the most common elements used in semiconductor technology.

q: Metals such as gold, silver, copper, brass, aluminium etc., are good conductors.
e: These metals are well-known for their high electrical conductivity due to abundant free electrons.

q: Non-metals such as plastic, glass, rubber, wax, quartz, etc., are insulators.
e: These non-metallic materials are classic examples of electrical insulators.

q: Transistors and other electronic components are made from semiconductors.
e: The semiconductor properties of materials like silicon are essential for manufacturing transistors and electronic components.
